title: Saprotroph recycling: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Saprotrophic fungi turn dead wood into new growth. An FPGA CXL Type-3 card hosts 8-16 salvaged DDR4 RDIMMs from retired servers and takes over the aged chips' 'periphery intelligence': per-DIMM retention profiling, chipkill ECC, adaptive refresh and bad-row remap, so they serve as a slower tier. One board spin plus firmware, ~$800k in 24 months, with revenue from refurbished pools.
why: Supply axis: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reusing even 10% adds memory at ~10-20% of new DDR5 cost/bit with zero fab capex.

title: Eliminate the latch: impact-ionization gain diode on each bitline
idea: Replace the cross-coupled latch with one p-i-n diode per bitline biased just below breakdown, in a gated Geiger mode. The ~30-100 mV charge-share signal shifts its avalanche delay, so a '1' fires a rail-to-rail pulse within ~0.5 ns while a '0' does not, and a quench transistor resets it.
why: Replaces a 6-transistor SA with 1 diode and 1 quench device (SA area -70%), and the sense charge is only a few fC. Dark counts, jitter and temperature drift are the risks.

title: Po: one device is a sense amp — tunnel-diode Goto latch
idea: Po: a sense amplifier made of one device. Replace the ~10-transistor cross-coupled latch with a series Goto pair of resonant/Esaki tunnel diodes per bitline, biased by a clocked supply so the midpoint snaps to one of its two NDR-stable states as set by the few-mV charge-sharing signal; a single pass transistor writes the snapped state back for restore.
why: Periphery (#7): SA strip area shrinks ~50-60%, which buys shorter bitlines (more SA strips per mm) for ~1.5x signal; ps-class NDR switching also trims tRCD.

title: Backside-built sense amplifiers connect through bitline-pitch nano-vias
idea: Worse: lay periphery beside the array where it eats half the die. Flip: after the front-side array, bond to a carrier, thin to under a micron as in backside power delivery, and layer-transfer low-temperature transistors for sense amps and sub-wordline drivers onto the backside, contacting bitlines through nano-vias at bitline pitch.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): folding periphery under the array shrinks die ~35-40% and raises bits per wafer without litho scaling.

title: Print-on-die carbon-nanotube TFT layer hosts slow control logic
idea: Worse: spend DRAM silicon on mode registers, BIST engines, temperature sensors and power-up sequencers that run at kHz-MHz. Flip: after passivation, inkjet-print a low-temperature carbon-nanotube TFT circuit layer on top of the die to host those slow functions, wired down through pad openings.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~5-10% of die moved off silicon onto a cheap printed layer.

title: Nesting: sub-wordline drivers built inside the array's vertical-transistor process
idea: TRIZ #7 Nesting: sub-wordline driver transistors are made as vertical-channel devices in the same pillar and buried-wordline steps as the cells, nested in a dummy-row band inside each mat, so the separate SWD stripes of planar logic transistors and their array-to-periphery boundary rules vanish.
why: Fact 7: SWD stripes are ~8-10% of die; nesting removes ~70% of that area and its extra masks, about a 6% die shrink per node with no lithography change.

title: Prior counteraction: data-aware counter-kick cancels bitline coupling before sensing
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: a small per-bank row-history cache predicts the neighbouring bitlines' data for the row about to open, and the precharge circuit injects a calibrated counter-charge through dedicated coupling caps so the worst-case bitline-to-bitline coupling during amplification is cancelled in advance.
why: Facts 1 and 8: recovers the ~20-30% of sense margin lost to coupling, allowing open-bitline layouts without twisting or ~25% smaller cell signal.

title: Dumb-die DRAM moves DLL, training and refresh logic to controller
idea: Periphery logic on a DRAM process costs 3-4 logic generations more per transistor. Strip the DRAM die to array, sense and simple I/O; the controller on a leading logic node owns clock deskew (forwarded clock), PHY training, ECC, refresh scheduling and row-hammer tracking.
why: Periphery share of die (fact 7) falls by ~8-15 points; logic moves to where transistors are ~10x cheaper.

title: Po: an array die that cannot decode
idea: Po: an array die that knows no addresses. Row/column predecoding, redundancy CAMs, refresh counters and command logic move to a hybrid-bonded logic-node base die, which drives pre-decoded one-hot group selects through ~1 um-pitch bonds; the array die keeps only sub-wordline drivers, SAs and final pass gates.
why: Periphery (#7): array-die periphery drops from ~49% to ~25-30%, ~35% more bits per array wafer, while the moved logic is ~5x denser on a logic node.

title: Dumb-array DRAM: CXL controller absorbs refresh, ECC, repair, test
idea: Hyperscalers already own smart memory controllers, so strip the DRAM die to cells, SAs, decoders and a narrow I/O; refresh scheduling, row-hammer tracking, ECC, repair remapping, mode registers and BIST move into a CXL controller on a logic node. With no random logic left, the DRAM die needs no EUV.
why: Periphery 49% -> ~30% (fact 7), and the DRAM die can be made in DUV-only fabs.

title: Touchscreen mutual-capacitance sensing reads cells nondestructively
idea: Borrowed from projected-capacitive touch controllers: each cell is a coupling capacitor at a wordline-bitline crossing on glass whose value is shifted by a trapped-charge or ferroelectric layer; a TX pulse on the wordline and charge sensing on the bitline read it without discharging any storage node.
why: Destructive read (fact 8): no restore write-back on read and far less refresh, roughly halving read energy, built from thin films on any substrate.

title: Skipping: precharge-free rail sensing with auto-zeroed reference sample
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: the equalize/precharge phase is skipped; each bitline stays at the rail it was last restored to, a coupling capacitor samples that level, and the sense amp compares the next cell's charge-sharing step against the sample plus a half-signal kick, alternating polarity each cycle.
why: Facts 7 and 8: equalizers and the VBL/2 generator disappear (~5% periphery area), tRP leaves the critical path (~15-20% shorter row cycle) and ~10% activation energy is saved.

title: Po: bitline capacitance is negative — active NIC cancellation
idea: Po: a bitline that pretends to be shorter. A small positive-feedback negative-impedance converter (cross-coupled Si MOS pair driving a coupling capacitor) at the bitline end synthesizes about -0.5 Cb during charge sharing, so the cell sees half the load and develops ~2x the voltage signal.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~2x signal, or Cs ~50% lower, or twice the cells per bitline (half the SA strips), with plain Si CMOS and no exotic dielectric.

title: Smoke detector: leaky analog charge counters catch row hammer
idea: Smoke builds up in an ionization chamber until the alarm trips. Give each group of 4 rows one tiny capacitor in the wordline-driver strip that gets a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a ~64 ms time constant; a comparator trips at ~500 activations' worth of charge and queues a targeted neighbour refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9, ~1k activation threshold): replaces SRAM counter tables and TRR logic with ~3 transistors plus 1 cap per 4 rows, monitors every row so it cannot be evaded by many-sided patterns, and costs <1% die.

title: Stochastically doped nanowire decoders discovered rather than drawn
idea: Ideal result: a decoder that needs no lithographic precision. Grow wordline-select nanowires with random axial doping segments that form random but unique codes against a coarse address mesh; at test, map which code selects which row into a table and accept a few percent unusable rows.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4) and periphery area (fact 7): replaces EUV-pitch decoders with self-assembled ones at cell pitch.

title: Bistable buckled-nanobeam cell read by a single pull-up
idea: Inverting 'the bit is an electrical state': each bit is the up/down position of a buckled nanobeam that touches a contact only when down; reading is an ohmic open-or-short, so a weak pull-up and an inverter replace the sense amp, with zero leakage and no refresh.
why: Near-infinite on/off ratio removes sense-margin problems and all refresh energy; periphery becomes trivial. Contact wear and stiction limit endurance (~1e10-1e12).

title: Another dimension: 512-tier vertical charge-coupled strings with one sense node
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: bits are charge packets in potential wells along a vertical oxide-semiconductor channel gated by 512 stacked wordline plates, a one-hole 3D-NAND-like process with no capacitor and no per-bit transistor. Reads clock the packets CCD-style down the pillar into one floating-diffusion sense node under the array, which regenerates them and re-injects them at the top, so refresh is just recirculation.
why: 100x path: NAND-like cost (~$0.05-0.15/GB) because periphery is one sense node per 512 bits, no EUV and few masks per tier; trade-offs: serial 10-50 us page access, and charge-transfer inefficiency and dark current cap string length, so a small DRAM cache must front it. Attacks Facts 1, 2, 4 and 7.

title: Elephantnose-fish impedance spectroscopy fixture catching counterfeit DRAM
idea: Elephantnose fish identify objects by how they distort a self-made electric field. A low-cost fixture sweeps tiny AC signals (10 kHz-1 GHz) across each DRAM package's pins and matches the impedance spectrum to genuine-die references, flagging remarked, recycled or wrong-die parts in seconds. VNA-based fixture plus reference database, ~$350k in 12 months.
why: Supply axis: in a 4x price spike, grey-market fakes surge. Trusted screening lets OEMs safely tap secondary supply.

title: Leaky integrator capacitor counts activations in analog
idea: Fuse a charge-deposit circuit into each sub-wordline driver group: every ACT dumps a fixed charge packet onto a small capacitor that leaks with a ~64 ms time constant, and when its voltage crosses a comparator threshold the group's neighbor rows get refreshed. It is a row-hammer counter with no SRAM or digital logic.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): per-row-group tracking for under 1% area, versus large CAM/SRAM counter tables; works on any process.

title: Series negative-capacitance HZO capacitor as passive bitline amplifier
idea: Substitute part of the transistor gain with a passive voltage step-up: a doped-HZO capacitor biased in its negative-capacitance region sits in series between the bitline and the latch input, so the transient voltage at the latch is amplified ~2-5x. It is buildable with ALD and e-beam in a university fab.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): if verified, the same latch resolves with ~2x less cell charge, relaxing capacitor aspect ratio.

title: Clocked resonant-tunneling-diode pair as monostable-bistable bitline sense element
idea: Effect: resonant tunneling and negative differential resistance. Two series RTDs (Si/SiGe interband or InGaAs/AlAs) form a MOBILE: ramping the clock bias moves the pair from monostable to bistable, and the bitline current imbalance on the middle node decides which RTD drops into its valley. NDR gives regenerative gain with 2 devices at ~0.3 V.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and SA area (fact 7): sensing at 0.3-0.5 V cuts SA-stripe CV^2 ~4x, using 2 devices instead of ~8.

title: Back-gate-pulsed dual-gate IGZO sense amplifiers
idea: Dual-gate IGZO SA transistors (<=350 C) get their back gate pulsed to +2 V only during the ~2-3 ns sense window, MAGNIFYING drive current ~3x, and parked at -1 V otherwise, MINIFYING leakage.
why: Facts 3 and 10: closes most of the oxide-versus-Si speed gap for over-array SAs while keeping periphery standby leakage near zero.

title: Chopper-measured sense offsets stored in a per-stripe trim row
idea: 1940s chopper-stabilized amplifiers swapped their inputs to cancel drift. During refresh slots each sense amp's inputs are shorted and swapped and its decisions counted, giving a 2-bit offset estimate per amp. The estimates are kept in a dedicated trim row and loaded into per-amp dynamic trim capacitors, which are rewritten with each refresh. Zero added masks.
why: Mismatch-driven sense-amp area halves (fact 7) and margin improves ~30 mV, extending bitlines or shrinking Cs (fact 1).

title: Inductive coupling links replace TSVs in hot memory stacks
idea: At 125 C, Cu TSVs suffer protrusion and voiding under thermal cycling and add keep-out zones; inductive coil links (contactless, ~1 Gb/s per coil) carry data between stacked dies with no metal through silicon. Power still uses a few large TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): ~2x less area per bit, no TSV yield loss, reliable 10 y at hot.

title: Idle sense amps run backward as distributed charge pumps
idea: Reverse the latch's job: during standby and refresh gaps, two extra switches per SA reconfigure the cross-coupled latches plus bitline capacitance into a distributed switched-capacitor doubler that tops up VPP/VBB right beside the wordline drivers.
why: Facts 7 and 10: central charge pumps and their decap (~5-8% of die) shrink, and local generation removes IR drop on the 3 V wordline rail.

title: Pixel-style bonded sense amps on every 256-cell bitline
idea: Scale jump from stacked CMOS image sensors (one bonded readout per pixel) to DRAM: hybrid-bond the array wafer to a 28 nm periphery wafer at 0.5 um pitch so every ~9 um (256-cell) bitline gets its own sense amp directly beneath it, instead of 1024-cell bitlines ending in edge SA stripes. The array die becomes pure cells; SAs, sub-wordline drivers and decoders all sit on the cheap wafer below.
why: Cbl drops ~3-4x so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~1.5-2 fF (capacitor AR ~60:1 -> ~25:1, fact 1), and the ~49% periphery leaves the expensive array die (fact 7); est. 25-35% lower cost per bit.

title: Excimer-laser LTPS decoders built monolithically above the cell array
idea: Smartphone OLED backplanes make ~100 cm2/Vs LTPS TFTs by excimer-laser annealing; a laser-crystallized poly-Si layer above the bitlines hosts row decoders and SWD logic at DUV rules, moving them out of the silicon area beside the array.
why: Decoder and SWD area beside the mats (~10% of die) reclaimed without EUV; the laser anneal's thermal budget stays local.

title: Plasma-display memory effect: global sustain waveform replaces refresh and transistors
idea: Failure mined: plasma displays held each pixel's state as wall charge under a global AC sustain waveform, with only row and column drivers and no per-pixel transistor, and lost to LCD and OLED on power. Fix: each crosspoint cell pairs a thin threshold switch with a small capacitor in a hysteresis loop. A global sustain clock re-pumps every 1 cell while 0 cells never fire, and coincident row/column pulses set or clear individual cells.
why: 10x at the same cost: no access transistor, refresh controller or refresh bandwidth. 4F^2 cells in 4 self-aligned decks sharing lines (~6x) x periphery shrinking to ~20% (~1.6x) = ~10x.

title: Mandate hammer-threshold grading so retired DIMMs re-enter service
idea: Effect: wordline-coupling disturbance (row-hammer first-flip count, HCfirst). Policy plus small lab: before hyperscaler DIMMs are shredded, a standard FPGA test measures each module's HCfirst and retention spread; modules get grades (e.g., hammer-tolerant, read-mostly cache tier) under an OCP spec and are resold, with reuse tax credits.
why: Usable supply: datacenters retire DRAM after 4-6 years while most cells are healthy; recovering 20% of retired DDR4/DDR5 adds supply with zero fab capex.

title: Eliminate decoder transistors: Schottky diode-matrix row decoding
idea: Build row predecode and decode as a classic diode-AND matrix of NiSi/n-Si Schottky diodes formed by self-aligned silicidation (unreacted Ni stripped in H2SO4/H2O2). Each decode node is dynamically precharged and pulled down by diodes on the complement address lines, so only the final wordline driver remains a transistor.
why: Cuts decoder transistor count ~70% and removes ~2 masks of gate and contact work in the decode zone, all etch-free (fact 7).

title: Avalanche-multiplying sense junction gives charge gain before latch
idea: Effect: impact-ionization avalanche multiplication. Transfer cell charge into a small guard-ringed n+/p junction biased just below breakdown in linear mode; injected carriers are multiplied ~10-30x, then the packet is quenched and integrated on the SA node, so gain comes before any transistor offset.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): ~10x charge gain would allow ~0.5-1 fF cells and faster sensing.

title: Wafer-on-wafer memory with no PHY, DLL, or pads
idea: Scale jump from die to wafer: bond a whole DRAM wafer face-to-face onto the accelerator wafer so each mat talks to logic through sub-um bonds; there are no DQ drivers, DLLs, ESD diodes, pads or SerDes, and defective mats are bypassed by wafer-level rerouting.
why: Removes ~10-15% of die area in I/O and clocking periphery (fact 7), cuts data movement to ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM (fact 5), with no TSV tax (fact 6).

title: Na: sodium-silicate water glass bonds periphery dies onto arrays
idea: Bond periphery dies face-to-face onto array wafers with a nanometer-thin sodium silicate adhesive cured at ~200 C, with Cu pillars electroplated through it and SiN barriers locking the Na; no argon/N2 plasma activation or argon-sputtered seed is needed.
why: Cheap, rare-gas-free die-to-wafer stacking moves periphery off the array die (fact 7) at lower capital than hybrid-bond tools and eases the TSV tax (fact 6).

title: Processor-hosted sense amps make memory dies pure cell fabric
idea: Ideal result: the memory die holds nothing but bits. Hybrid-bond a cell-only die face-to-face onto the accelerator die, which carries all sense amps, decoders and row buffers in advanced logic at ~1 um bond pitch, so data never crosses a PHY.
why: Facts 5, 7: memory die area per bit drops ~45% and data movement falls to ~0.1 pJ/bit; the cell fab needs no periphery process.

title: Quadruplex telegraph bitlines carry two cells per sense event
idea: Copy Edison's 1874 quadruplex telegraph, which sent one message as current polarity and another as amplitude on a single wire. Two cells on paired rows share one bitline event: one dumps charge through its normal access device, and the other is read through a 2x plate-line pulse that injects a doubly weighted, opposite-polarity charge. A 4-level sense (two latches with offset references) decodes both bits.
why: Halves sense amps per bit and halves activation events per bit read (facts 7, 8): ~1.6x periphery density.

title: Move the bits, not the sensor: one read head per track
idea: Inverting 'every bit sits still and sensing comes to it': 64 bits are stored as magnetic domains along a vertical nanowire and shifted by current pulses past a single MTJ read head at the track base, so one sense amp and one access device serve 64 bits.
why: Sense-amp and access-device count drop ~64x, magnetic state has unlimited endurance and no refresh; shift latency of ~10-30 ns keeps it DRAM-class for row-buffered access.

title: Deep Space Network weak-signal sensing frees capacitors from wet mold-strip
idea: NASA hears Voyager's 20 W transmitter by building great receivers, not louder transmitters. Correlated double sampling (sample the bitline after equalize and after charge share, subtract on a capacitor pair) plus a low-noise preamp resolves ~15 mV, so cells can use a ~1.5 fF, ~15:1 dry-etched capacitor instead of a 70:1 cylinder that needs a wet HF mold-oxide strip and many high-AR rinse/dry cycles.
why: Water and the capacitor wall: the mold strip, stiction-safe rinse/IPA dry and high-AR cleans, among DRAM's most UPW-hungry steps, fall ~10x; capacitor-module steps fall ~40%.

title: Controller-held repair map deletes on-die fuses and compare logic
idea: Repair information is only (#faulty rows x log2 N) bits, a few kbit, yet fuse banks and address comparators cost percent-level die area. Ship dies with no redundancy steering; the bad-row/column map measured at test is stored in the module SPD and the host controller remaps physical addresses.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~3-5% die area recovered; repairs become updatable in field.

title: Eliminate metal etching: anodization-defined aluminum periphery wiring
idea: Deposit blanket Al, mask the line regions with PAG-free DNQ/novolak i-line resist, and anodize the exposed metal fully into Al2O3 in citric or boric acid. The converted oxide becomes the insulator between lines, giving a planar wiring level with no metal etch, no gap fill and no CMP.
why: Removes etch, fill and CMP from 2-3 periphery signal levels using abundant Al (no W, Cu or Ta), and the planar levels ease stacking.

title: One sense-amp layer serves every tier via vertical bitlines
idea: Rearrange the scaling direction: in monolithic 3D DRAM grown with U.S.-built deposition and etch tools (no EUV), bitlines run vertically through N tiers to a single SA layer below, chosen by tier-select transistors, so periphery stays constant while bits grow N-fold.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery share falls roughly as 1/N with tiers; density comes from deposition, not U.S.-unavailable lithography.

title: Photographic-development tunnel-diode latch amplifies latent bitline charge
idea: Borrow film development, which amplifies a latent image of a few silver atoms by ~10^9: place a Goto pair of Esaki tunnel diodes on each bitline pair, biased near the peak of its N-shaped I-V. A few millivolts of cell signal tips it into one valley state in picoseconds, and a CMOS restore stage follows.
why: NDR latch offset is set by junction doping, not gate litho, and it switches at ~0.3-0.5 V: ~3x smaller usable bitline signal and lower array voltage, attacking both the charge wall and the CV^2 voltage floor.

title: Thermal circuit-breaker integrator tracks row hammer analogically
idea: Borrowed from bimetal thermal breakers: each wordline driver has a tiny leaky capacitor that gets a fixed charge quantum per activation and bleeds with a ~64 ms time constant; when a threshold comparator trips, it requests a neighbor refresh.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~1k-activation thresholds with ~2 transistors and 1 capacitor per row instead of SRAM counter tables, ~0.5% area.

title: Per-driver BEOL bootstrap capacitor self-boosts every wordline
idea: Each wordline driver gets a local high-k MIM bootstrap capacitor (<=300 C) that capacitively lifts the selected wordline above VDD at the moment of selection, MINIFYING the global VPP network and its pump to a small reserve.
why: Facts 7 and 10: VPP distribution and pump area -60%, wordline energy -30% because only the selected line is boosted.

title: Venus-flytrap analog leaky integrators as row-hammer counters
idea: The Venus flytrap counts touches with a decaying calcium signal (two within ~30 s closes the trap). Each 8-row group gets a DRAM-process capacitor that takes a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a designed time constant near the refresh window. Crossing a comparator threshold triggers neighbor refresh, with no SRAM counters or CAM.
why: Fact 9: digital per-row counters cost ~1-2% of die and energy. An analog leaky counter is ~3 transistors plus one cell-type cap per group (~10x smaller) and forgets old activity by itself.

title: FD-SOI back-gate voltages null sense-amp offset on a 22FDX shuttle
idea: Effect: body effect through the buried oxide. On an FD-SOI MPW, each SA pair's back gate is tied to a small hold capacitor that an auto-zero loop charges during a calibration slot; the ~80 mV/V body coefficient nulls offset and re-calibrates every refresh period, tracking aging and temperature.
why: SA area (fact 7): minimum-size SA devices (4-8x smaller) become usable; GF 22FDX in New York gives a U.S. path for a fabless team.

title: Thirty-two-cell averaged reference minifies reference error
idea: MAGNIFY the reference: each mat's sense reference is generated by charge-averaging 32 dummy cells written half 0 and half 1 at every refresh, so it tracks process, temperature and leakage with sqrt(32) less random error than a single dummy.
why: Fact 1: recovers ~20-30% of sense margin, convertible into smaller Cs or longer refresh intervals (Fact 3).

title: Vertical NAND-structured DRAM strings with shadow-page sequential read
idea: Failure mined: Toshiba's 1993 NAND-structured DRAM put cells in series to eliminate contacts, but died because cells had to be read and restored in strict order. Fix: build 64-cell vertical strings in a 3D-NAND-style stack (word planes deposited and etched once, a thin capacitor at each tier) and treat each string as one burst. A shadow latch page in bonded periphery reads it out sequentially and restores it in reverse order.
why: 10x at the same cost: 64 tiers from one channel-hole etch (3D NAND cost structure, ~1 EUV layer), with one contact and one sense amp per string, give ~10-15x bits/mm^2 at similar wafer cost. A 64-bit string matches cache-line bursts.

title: Backside 1064 nm illumination accelerates DRAM retention screening
idea: Effect: photoconductive carrier generation. A benchtop station floods bare dies (or windowed package backs) with calibrated 1064 nm light, which passes through silicon and adds a uniform, dose-set generation current to every storage junction. A known added leakage turns a long retention wait into minutes, and the dose-response slope separates leaky cells from merely marginal ones.
why: Test capital/time (fact 4): 5-10x shorter retention screens cut tester capex per bit and enable fine retention binning for low-refresh SKUs; one optics bench plus an existing tester.

title: Pulsed back-plate biasing replaces 3 V thick-oxide wordline drivers
idea: Substitute the boosted ~3 V wordline with a buried back plate under each mat that is pulsed during access to lower the access-transistor Vt and held negative during retention. Wordlines then swing only ~1.2 V through thin-oxide drivers.
why: Voltage floor and periphery area (facts 7, 10): drivers shrink ~3x, charge-pump load drops sharply, and wordline CV^2 falls ~6x.

title: Ferroelectric back-gate trim cancels sense-amp offset for 30 years
idea: For 30-year industrial controllers that can never be replaced, each SA transistor pair gets an HZO back-gate whose polarization stores a per-SA threshold trim, programmed at wafer test and re-tuned in the field by a BIST that measures offset. Static mismatch and slow NBTI drift are both nulled.
why: Margin needed falls from ~100 mV to ~30 mV, enabling ~2-3x smaller Cs or longer bitlines, and minimum-size SA devices (facts 1, 7).

title: Charlieplexed wordline decode with bidirectional selector pairs
idea: Hobbyists drive N(N-1) LEDs from N pins by Charlieplexing with tri-state polarity. Hang each sub-wordline driver gate between an ordered pair of predecode lines through a polarity-sensitive diode-like BEOL selector, so 24 tri-state predecode lines address 552 drivers instead of a full NAND decoder per row.
why: Water via area: row-decode area falls ~10x (decoders ~8-10% of die to <1%), cutting the wafers, and hence the water, attributable to decoding ~10x; die area -8%.

title: Low-barrier volatile MRAM refreshed by stock DRAM periphery
idea: Inverting 'MRAM must be nonvolatile': thin free layers with an energy barrier of ~20-30 kT keep data for ms to seconds and switch with ~10x less current, and the existing DRAM refresh controller periodically re-writes them while TMR sensing reads them.
why: Unlimited magnetic endurance with fJ-class writes and tiny cells, reusing DRAM's refresh and timing periphery unchanged; no capacitor.

title: NEMS contact-switch access device with true zero off-current
idea: Scale jump from MEMS relays to ~20 nm: the access transistor is replaced by a nano-electromechanical contact switch with a vacuum gap when off, so the storage node leaks only through the capacitor dielectric and surfaces, giving hours of retention; refresh is omitted and data idle longer moves to NV.
why: Removes the subthreshold/GIDL leakage tail (fact 3) entirely -> zero refresh; contact wear and ~ns pull-in are the risks.

title: VCMA-gated shared spin-orbit write lines: one driver per row
idea: Constraint: non-volatile SOT-MRAM, whose large write drivers swell periphery. Run one heavy-metal SOT current line under an entire row of MTJs and select which bits switch with voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy on each MTJ's top electrode, so a single row driver plus low-current column voltage gates replace per-column write drivers.
why: Periphery area: write-driver silicon -70-80%; SOT keeps read and write paths separate, which gives reads effectively unlimited endurance.

title: Reusable donor wafers supply periphery silicon via layer transfer
idea: Ideal result: silicon that is used ten times. Grow periphery device layers on a porous-silicon or SiGe release substrate, transfer the thin layer onto the bonded memory stack, then polish and reuse the donor wafer.
why: Scarce resources: cuts virgin wafer and Spruce Pine quartz crucible demand for periphery tiers ~5-10x.

title: Copying: optical readout of stacked electro-optic charge films
idea: TRIZ #26 Copying replaces per-bit silicon sensing with an optical copy: bits are charge in a transistor-free photoconductor/electro-optic film stack (like optically addressed light modulators), written by a micro-LED projector and read by a CMOS image sensor that selects one of 32 films through wavelength-selective layers; refresh is re-projecting the captured image.
why: 100x path: the storage films cost cents per m2 and one image sensor plus micro-LED array serves 32 films and millions of bits per frame; trade-offs: 1-10 us frame latency, optical volume, ms retention requiring constant re-copy, and interlayer crosstalk. Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Drop row-hammer counters; let flips land inside ECC budget
idea: Box: standard cap x Si access x standard SA x no TRR or counter logic x bulk Si x standard. Target-row-refresh trackers and per-row activation counters are removed; a randomized background scrub plus the 1%-capable code absorb hammer flips, and a simple activation-rate cap keeps them under 0.1% of a codeword.
why: Periphery: row-hammer tracker SRAM and logic (growing as the threshold falls to ~1k) removed, with code margin as the defense.

title: Potluck cookbook: open-source, silicon-proven DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: A potluck works because everyone shares recipes. Fund an open-source library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps with offset calibration, row-hammer trackers, pumps, LPDDR/DDR5 PHYs) with silicon-proven layouts on U.S. 28/22 nm processes, so startups and foundries can build memory dies without decades of trade-secret circuit know-how.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery know-how is a hidden entry barrier; shared IP could cut a new entrant's design cost from ~$500M to ~$50-100M and save ~2 years.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops 180 nm periphery blocks into array wafers
idea: Borrow 1990s fluidic self-assembly (Alien Technology, 1994): make charge pumps, I/O, fuse/test and command logic as trapezoidal ~50 um blocks on depreciated 180 nm lines. Pour them as a slurry over the array wafer, whose etched recesses accept only the matching shape, then wire them with one coarse i-line metal layer.
why: Moves the ~20-25% of die that is not pitch-matched periphery off the leading-edge wafer onto ~$600 200 mm wafers made in U.S. fabs: ~25% more bits per expensive wafer and more U.S. content.

title: Plasma-panel sustain waveform refreshes cells without sensing
idea: AC plasma displays (1964) held every pixel with nothing but a global sustain pulse and wall-charge bistability. Give each cell a series threshold-switching selector (e.g., NbOx) to a global pulsed sustain rail: cells still above threshold (decaying 1s) conduct and are topped up, and cells near zero stay off. The whole array refreshes in one global pulse, with no row activation and no sense amp.
why: Eliminates refresh activations (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) and the refresh counter and scheduler logic; claims >10x lower refresh energy.

title: Column-parallel single-slope ADC reads two bits per cell
idea: Borrowed from image-sensor column ADCs: one global voltage ramp is broadcast to all 8k columns of a mat, and each column's tiny comparator latches a shared Gray-code counter when the ramp crosses its bitline. Each cell stores four charge levels and is digitized in one ~8 ns ramp.
why: Density and cost per bit: 2 bits/cell for ~15% extra periphery, because the per-column cost is one comparator plus two latches instead of three sense amps.

title: IGZO charge-coupled readout drains rows to few sense nodes
idea: MAGNIFY serialization: like a CCD image sensor, a row's charge packets are shifted bucket-brigade along BEOL IGZO transfer gates (<=350 C) to one floating-diffusion sense node per 64 columns, MINIFYING sense amps 64x for sequential tensor streams.
why: Fact 7: periphery area in stream banks -50%; IGZO's tiny leakage keeps packets intact during transfer, but transfer inefficiency is the risk.

title: Fuse-less DRAM: host controller holds the repair map
idea: Reverse who repairs: the die ships without fuse/antifuse banks or address-compare redundancy logic; failing rows and columns are recorded in a signed on-module SPD map at test, and the memory controller or OS remaps them to spare rows at boot.
why: Fact 7: removes fuse banks, redundancy comparators and post-package-repair circuits (~3-5% die); spare rows become ordinary capacity when unused.

title: Roundabout traffic: self-timed completion detection per mat
idea: Like a roundabout letting cars go as soon as the way is clear instead of waiting for a fixed signal cycle, each SA latch drives a dual-rail done signal, and a per-mat completion tree releases column access when that mat's slowest SA resolves, not after the chip's worst-case tRCD.
why: Latency/bandwidth: average tRCD falls ~25-35% by reclaiming PVT guard-bands.

title: Old-node DRAM arrays bonded to 40nm periphery in CIS fabs
idea: Strip the periphery from 2x-nm DRAM array designs still running in depreciated lines, and hybrid-bond those wafers face-to-face to 40/28 nm logic periphery wafers using the wafer-to-wafer bonding lines that image-sensor fabs already run at volume; SAs connect through ~1-2 um pitch pads per bitline-pair group.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): ~1.6x bits per wafer from old DRAM lines with no new fab, using idle 28-40 nm logic and existing CIS bonding tools.

title: Embargo periphery: 65 nm US wafers bonded under the array
idea: A Soviet engineer denied EUV builds what the old fab can make. Put all sense amps, drivers and decoders on a separate 65-40 nm DUV wafer from an existing U.S. trailing-edge fab, relax their pitch with 4:1 bitline multiplexers on the array wafer, and hybrid-bond the two at ~1 um pitch.
why: Takes periphery off the EUV wafer (fact 4), uses depreciated idle U.S. capacity (U.S. manufacturability), and returns ~49% of array-wafer area to cells (fact 7).

title: Avalanche-photodiode charge multiplier at the bitline foot
idea: Borrowed from avalanche photodiodes and photomultipliers: a gated impact-ionization junction at the sense node multiplies the few thousand electrons dumped by the cell 10-30x before the latch fires, the way an APD amplifies single photons. A ~1 ns bias pulse limits dark current to the sensing window.
why: Charge wall (facts 1-2): a 0.3-0.5 fF capacitor at AR ~15:1 gives today's signal, removing the 60-75:1 pillar etch and making stackable 3D capacitors viable.

title: Latch-resolution time flags convert errors into cheap erasures
idea: A weak (hot, leaky) cell produces a small signal and the latch resolves slowly; a timing comparator per SA group marks bits that resolved late as erasures. Reed-Solomon/BCH corrects 2 erasures for the cost of 1 error, so soft information is free.
why: ~2x stronger correction at the same parity, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C or smaller Cs (facts 1, 3).

title: Bit-significance-tiered sense amps: big for MSBs, tiny for LSBs
idea: KV-cache and weight tensors tolerate errors in low mantissa bits: columns mapped to sign and exponent bits get large offset-compensated SAs, while LSB columns get minimum-size latches running at ~1e-4 BER with relaxed refresh. The controller fixes the bit-to-column layout.
why: SA area -30% and refresh energy -40% on AI-tier dies (facts 3, 7) with negligible model-accuracy loss.

title: Minify the fab: 400 C-only periphery add-on lines in U.S.
idea: Build $1-2B BEOL-only lines (no furnaces, epi, implanters or EUV) near U.S. packaging sites that add IGZO periphery, row-buffer and repair tiers onto array wafers bought from any supplier, capturing roughly half of die value domestically.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~1/8 the capex of a full DRAM fab and ~18-month build versus 3-5 years.

title: Roll-to-roll anodized alumina templates for ultra-high-aspect capacitors
idea: Worse: keep the cell signal tiny so sense amps must stay large and bitlines short. Flip: grow nanoporous anodic alumina continuously on a roll-to-roll aluminum line, transfer the AR>200 pore film onto the array, and ALD-coat the pores into capacitors, with storage-node pads wider than the pore pitch so each node captures several pores.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): AR 115+ without deep etch; more signal lets sense amps shrink and bitlines lengthen.

title: Nantero's nanotubes as BEOL periphery transistors, not memory cells
idea: Failure mined: Nantero NRAM stalled on CNT-fabric switching variability. Fix: use aligned CNT films as BEOL CNFETs made below 400 C. A wide device averages over hundreds of tubes, so variability only has to meet logic-level tolerance. Row predecoders, column muxes and secondary sense stages are then built above the capacitor array.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7). Moving even half of it over the array gives ~1.3-1.4x more bits per wafer with no new EUV layers, using a domestic, tungsten-free device stack.

title: Zero offset budget: floating-gate trimmed sense amps
idea: Limit: sense amp offset must be zero. Each SA's cross-coupled pair includes a small charge-trap trim transistor programmed once at wafer test, from an on-die BIST measurement, to null that SA's own Vt mismatch, recovering ~15-20 mV of margin.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): the recovered margin lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3 fF (AR 70 to 45), so capacitor etch and deposition get cheaper, ~10-15% cost/bit.

title: Stencil spray-paint: shadow-mask deposition of periphery pads and power
idea: Like a graffiti stencil, deposit the periphery's wide top-level features (pads, power straps, redistribution at >=2 um) through a reusable silicon-nitride MEMS stencil held in proximity during sputtering or evaporation. No resist, develop, strip or post-etch clean.
why: Water: top-metal/pad litho, etch and clean sequences (~30-50 L UPW per layer) fall ~10x, and those layers cost a fraction to pattern.

title: Po: every bitline wears a shield — coaxial poly-Si bitlines
idea: Po: a bitline wrapped like a TV cable. Form bitlines inside a grounded conformal doped poly-Si sleeve separated by an SiO2/air liner, so neighbor-bitline coupling and wordline kickback terminate on the shield; Cb rises ~15% but pattern-dependent noise (up to ~30% of sense margin) disappears.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and density: ~15% net margin gain and tighter bitline pitch, using Si, O, N only.

title: Self-service: read-write-read self-reference removes matched sense amp pairs
idea: TRIZ #25 Self-service: each read samples the bitline after charge sharing, writes a known '1', shares again and samples a second time, comparing the cell with itself on one capacitor pair; device mismatch, reference bitlines and dummy cells cancel, so sloppy TFT or 180 nm transistors can serve as the sense amp.
why: 100x path: sensing works with ~100 mV-offset cheap devices and single-ended bitlines on mature or TFT lines; trade-offs: ~3x longer read cycle and an extra write per read (energy and disturb). Attacks Facts 4 and 7.

title: Open array-periphery bond standard plus CHIPS grants
idea: Publish an open die-to-die standard that fixes the bitline-group, wordline and power pinout between DRAM array wafers and periphery wafers, and use CHIPS-style grants to have U.S. trailing logic fabs (90-22 nm) build the periphery tier for any array maker.
why: U.S. manufacturability (1-2% share): moves about half of each die's function into existing U.S. capacity without a new DRAM fab.

title: No fuses, no spare rows: ship DRAM with a signed defect map
idea: Inverting 'every die must look perfect': delete redundant rows/columns, fuse banks and repair logic; at test, write each die's failing 4 KB pages into a signed SPD defect map and have the memory controller or OS allocator skip them like NAND bad blocks.
why: Recovers ~5-8% die area plus repair test time and raises sellable yield, for ~6-10% lower cost per bit with low technical risk; needs controller/OS support.

title: High-voltage drivers on glass: TFT periphery on U.S. panels
idea: Reverse the substrate for high-voltage periphery: global wordline drivers, level shifters and pumps, which need 3-5 V rather than density, are built as TFTs on a U.S.-made glass interposer panel and connected to the array die through fine-pitch redistribution.
why: Fact 7 and capital: thick-oxide periphery (~8-10% of die) leaves the silicon; panel processing costs ~1/10 of silicon per area.

title: Anti-weight: switched negative capacitance cancels bitline load during sensing
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight counterbalances the dead weight of bitline capacitance: during the charge-sharing window a switched-capacitor negative-impedance converter (or a thin ferroelectric negative-capacitance layer in the bitline shield dielectric) presents about -0.7 CBL, so the cell sees ~30% of the physical bitline load; it is disconnected before restore to stay stable.
why: Fact 1: transfer ratio up ~3x, so storage capacitance can drop from ~5 fF to ~2 fF (aspect ratio ~30:1) or bitlines can be 3x longer with 3x fewer sense amps.

title: Pogo stick: ferroelectric negative capacitance cancels bitline load
idea: A pogo spring returns energy instead of absorbing it. Put a thin HZO negative-capacitance element in series at each SA input so the bitline-plus-NC network shows a much smaller effective capacitance during charge sharing, raising the signal per unit charge and letting the array run at ~0.4-0.5 V.
why: Effective C_BL ~3-5x lower and VARY ~2x lower give ~10x on bitline energy if a stable, hysteresis-free NC regime can be held; physics is unproven at speed.

title: Transient negative capacitance cancels bitline load only during sensing
idea: Failure mined: negative-capacitance FETs flopped because NC turned out to be hysteretic and stable only transiently. Fix: transient is all sensing needs. A thin HZO NC capacitor is switched in series with the bitline only for the ~3 ns charge-share window to partly cancel bitline capacitance, then disconnected before hysteresis matters.
why: The charge-share signal dV = Q/(Cs+Cbl,eff) grows ~2-4x, allowing ~2-3x smaller cell capacitors or 2x longer bitlines (half the SAs).

title: Three-terminal SOT cells give read-while-write banks
idea: Inverting 'reads and writes share one path': spin-orbit-torque cells have separate write (heavy-metal line) and read (MTJ) terminals, so each bank gets an independent read sense path and write driver and can serve a read and a write in the same cycle.
why: Removes write-to-read turnaround and bank conflicts, raising effective bandwidth ~20-40% without more banks; capacitor-free with unlimited endurance.

title: Po: banks chosen by pitch — AlN resonator select tones
idea: Po: a decoder that listens for its note. Each bank or subarray group enable is gated by an AlN thin-film acoustic resonator with a unique frequency on one shared RF select line; a single-tone burst wakes only the matching group through a rectifier, replacing trees of global decode wires and repeaters.
why: Periphery (#7): fewer global decode wires and repeaters and less routing congestion, using CMOS-compatible Al and N only.

title: LTPS display demux: one sense amp serves four bitlines
idea: Like the 1:3 demultiplexers that let one display source driver feed several columns, bitlines develop in parallel and hold their signal on their own capacitance while a BEOL switch tree steps one SA across four bitlines in ~1 ns slots, restoring each before moving on.
why: Periphery area: SA count falls 4x (SA stripe ~15% to ~5% of die) for ~+3 ns tRAS; nanosecond holding fits the leakage budget.

title: Bank-to-bank recycling of bitline restore charge
idea: When a bank precharges, its bitlines (half at VARY, half at ground) are not simply equalized to VBLP; a switch matrix first dumps the high-side charge into the reservoir feeding the next bank's restore, recycling about half the bitline charge.
why: Voltage floor and energy (fact 10): bitline swing dominates array energy; ~30-40% lower activation energy from a circuit-only change.

title: Paired banks swap bitline charge instead of dumping it
idea: Ideal result: bitline swings cost nothing because charge is borrowed and returned. When a bank precharges, its high bitlines connect through a shared bus to a second bank's bitlines that are about to precharge, so half that bank's charge comes from the first bank's discarded charge.
why: Energy (facts 8, 10): recovers ~25-40% of bitline activation energy, the largest term in random-access energy.

title: Matchstick: consume-once reads with decoupled sense amps skip restore
idea: A match is used once: add an isolation gate so the SA latches from a +/-100 mV bitline signal without driving the bitline rail to rail, and add a READ-CONSUME command; for data the host marks read-once (streamed KV cache, network buffers, transpose scratch) the row is left destroyed and marked free, so neither full swing nor restore happens.
why: Full-swing restore is >70% of activation energy; consume reads cut array energy ~10x and halve tRAS; needs a JEDEC/CXL command and OS tracking of dead rows.

title: Po: the row buffer survives power-off — FeB/MgO shadow latches
idea: Po: open rows that survive power-off. Pair each SA with a Co-free FeB/MgO/FeB magnetic tunnel junction shadow latch on Ti/TiN seeds, written as a row closes, so SA and decoder strips can be fully power-gated between bursts and the row buffer restored in nanoseconds on wake.
why: Idle power (#3 share): periphery leakage drops close to zero during idle while open-row hits are kept; Fe, B, Mg, O, Ti only.

title: Asymmetric-leakage data inversion keeps most cells in non-leaking state
idea: Effect: one-sided leakage (only charged cells decay toward error). An FPGA/CXL controller inverts each row's data whenever that leaves more cells discharged, using the module's true/anti-cell map learned once by a retention scan, and stores one inversion flag per row in spare metadata bits; zero-heavy data leaves ~70-90% of cells uncharged.
why: Refresh/reliability (fact 3): fewer charged cells means fewer retention failures, enabling ~2x longer refresh intervals at the same error rate; pure controller work.

title: Injection-locked oscillator pair turns bitline signal into phase decision
idea: Effect: sub-harmonic injection locking. Each SA stripe hosts a pair of tiny coupled ring oscillators pumped at their second harmonic, so they become phase-bistable (0 or 180 degrees, as in oscillator Ising machines); the bitline differential briefly biases the coupling, the pair locks into one phase, and a phase detector restores full swing. Gain comes from locking dynamics rather than transistor matching.
why: SA offset and area (facts 7, 10): a phase decision averages mismatch over many cycles, tolerating ~5x worse device matching and working near 0.5 V.

title: BEOL MTJ repair registers replace laser and eFuse banks
idea: MINIFY redundancy fuse area ~10x by storing repair addresses in BEOL magnetic tunnel junctions (annealed <=400 C) instead of laser fuses or eFuses, and MAGNIFY repair opportunities by reprogramming them in the field after aging or row-hammer damage.
why: Fact 7 (fuse banks and repair logic are several % of periphery) plus lifetime yield: weak rows can be swapped for spares over the product life.

title: Gleaner's cool tier: sense-marginal dies for liquid-cooled racks
idea: Farmers glean the field after harvest. Dies that fail sense margin only above ~75 C are binned as cool-tier DDR5/HBM, sold at standard JEDEC timings into liquid- and immersion-cooled racks that hold devices under 60 C.
why: Turns marginal yield loss into salable bits (+3-8% supply), exploiting how leakage and offset tighten when cool (fact 3).

title: Retention-class mats exposed as address bits
idea: Use test time as a time machine: at wafer test, hours-long 85 C dwells measure each mat's worst cell, tail cells are remapped to spare rows, and mats are binned into retention classes (0.1, 1, 10, 100 s) that the decoder exposes as high address bits; the allocator places each object only in a class longer than its maximum idle time, and refresh is never issued.
why: Zero refresh (fact 3) with no new materials, since median mats already hold data for seconds; retention variation becomes a product feature.

title: Dithered sense amps detect signals smaller than their offset
idea: Ideal result: a sense amp immune to its own noise. Inject controlled random dither into the SA reference and fire 8 fast mini-decisions on the shared bitline; majority counting extracts signals well below the static offset (stochastic resonance).
why: Charge wall (fact 1): allows ~2-3x smaller Cs at modest latency cost, suitable for capacity-tier memory.

title: Partial-charge sip read makes DRAM sensing non-destructive
idea: A tightly controlled subthreshold wordline pulse lets only ~3% of the cell charge (~450 e-) leak into a 0.2 fF local sense node; kT/C charge noise there is ~6 e-, so 450 e- is a >20 sigma signal (~0.36 V). The cell keeps 97% of its charge, so nothing is restored and only the addressed 64 B is sensed; normal refresh tops cells up.
why: Kills destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): per-useful-bit read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ; also removes row-activation hammer stress.
